common_name: Sweet Lifeberry Goji (Compact High-Yield Goji Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Sweet Lifeberry is a compact, patented goji selection bred as a sweeter-fruited sibling to 'Big Lifeberry' and stays smaller and tidier than seed-grown goji, making it suitable for large containers or foundation plantings.

directions: Sweet Lifeberry is a compact, self-fertile goji cultivar selected from breeding work aimed at improving fruit flavor and plant habit over wild-type Lycium barbarum, which is native to temperate Asia and naturalized widely across Europe. Unlike the sprawling, wide-arching canes of seedling goji, this selection forms a dense, rounded mound only a few feet tall, so it fits into smaller beds, patio containers, or low hedges rather than requiring the trellising many goji plants need. It flowers on new wood through summer, setting clusters of bright orange-red berries that ripen continuously into fall and are noticeably sweeter and less bitter than typical wild-collected goji. Grow it in full sun in lean, well-drained, even alkaline soil, and avoid overwatering or heavy fertility, both of which encourage rank, floppy growth at the expense of fruit.

planting.note: Plant grafted or budded trees in spring in ordinary, well-drained garden soil in full sun to light shade; this is a graft-derived bigeneric hybrid between hawthorn and medlar, so trees are propagated only vegetatively and true seedlings are not available.

directions: This unusual small tree originated in Bronvaux, France in the 1890s as a graft chimera or bud sport between hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna) and medlar (Mespilus germanica), and it displays traits of both parents on the same plant, sometimes even on the same branch. Leaves range from lobed, hawthorn-like foliage to broader medlar-type leaves, and the tree bears an abundance of small white spring flowers followed by a mix of small hawthorn-like haws and larger, true medlar fruits that require bletting (soft ripening after frost) before eating. It tolerates poor, chalky, or heavy soils better than plain medlar and needs little pruning beyond removing dead or crossing wood, making it a low-maintenance curiosity for collectors of unusual fruiting trees rather than a productive orchard crop. Because it is a graft hybrid rather than a stable botanical species, named specimens are propagated by grafting onto hawthorn or quince rootstock.

common_name: Golden Nugget Barberry (Very Dwarf Rounded Golden-Foliage Barberry)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun for the best gold color; Golden Nugget is one of the smallest thunbergii cultivars available and needs almost no shearing to hold its shape.

directions: Golden Nugget is an extremely dwarf, dense, mounding sport of Japanese barberry, forming a tidy little dome of bright yellow-gold foliage that emerges with a light orange-red tint in spring before deepening to gold through summer. Its diminutive scale makes it useful as a low edging plant, a rock-garden accent, or a repeated color note along a walkway where full-size barberries would quickly overwhelm the space. Like other thunbergii selections it carries small pale-yellow spring flowers and small red berries in fall, though its fruit set is typically light and secondary to its foliage display. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil once established and holds its compact form with little to no pruning, but gardeners should check state and local restrictions on Japanese barberry before planting, since the species has naturalized in parts of the eastern and midwestern United States.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun for the deepest purple foliage color; this vigorous hybrid needs more room than dwarf thunbergii cultivars and works well as an informal hedge or specimen.

directions: Berberis x ottawensis is a garden hybrid between Berberis thunbergii and the European Berberis vulgaris, and 'Superba' is its best-known selection, prized for large, rounded, deep reddish-purple leaves on a substantially bigger, more vigorous shrub than typical thunbergii cultivars. In spring it carries small pale-yellow flowers in short hanging clusters, more conspicuous than those of most purple-leaved barberries, followed by red berries that persist into winter and draw birds. Its arching, thorny stems make it effective as a barrier hedge, background shrub, or bold color contrast against green or gold foliage, and it colors best with full sun exposure. It is tolerant of a wide range of soils, including poor or dry ones, but appreciates good drainage, and because one parent is Japanese barberry, gardeners in regions with barberry restrictions should confirm local rules before planting.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; this low, spreading species is well suited to mixed borders or rock-garden slopes where its berry and autumn color display can be seen up close.

directions: Native to the mountains of western China, Berberis wilsoniae was collected in the early twentieth century by plant hunter Ernest Wilson and is grown for its combination of fine, blue-green summer foliage, brilliant orange and red autumn color, and abundant clusters of translucent coral-pink berries that ripen in fall and often persist after leaf drop. It forms a low, wide-spreading, thorny mound rather than an upright shrub, making it useful for the front of a border, a bank planting, or informal low hedging where its fruit display can be appreciated at eye level. Small pale-yellow flowers appear in spring but are secondary to the foliage and fruit interest that follow. It thrives in full sun with good drainage and tolerates dry, poor soils once established, needing little supplemental water or feeding in most garden situations.

common_name: Admiration Barberry (Dwarf Mounding Orange-Rimmed Gold Barberry)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest color contrast between the orange leaf margin and deep red-orange center; Admiration stays dense and mounded without shearing.

directions: Admiration is a compact, dwarf Japanese barberry selection bred for a distinctive two-tone leaf, with a deep red-orange center bordered by a bright golden-orange margin that intensifies through the growing season. Its tight, mounded habit and small mature size make it well suited to foundation plantings, mixed containers, or as a repeated low accent along a path, roles too small in scale for full-size barberry hedges. Small pale-yellow flowers appear along the thorny stems in spring, followed by a light set of red fall berries, though the plant is grown primarily for its long season of foliage color rather than fruit. It is drought- and heat-tolerant once established and holds its dense form with essentially no pruning, but as with other Japanese barberry cultivars, gardeners should check whether the species is restricted or discouraged in their state before planting.
sources: Proven Winners ColorChoice Shrubs plant information

common_name: Coastal Gold Ebbing's Silverberry (Gold-Centered Evergreen Elaeagnus)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun to partial shade; Coastal Gold was selected for extra tolerance of wind and salt exposure, making it a strong choice for seaside plantings and exposed hedgerows.

directions: Coastal Gold is a variegated selection of Ebbing's silverberry raised for improved resilience in exposed, windswept, salt-laden sites, an especially useful trait since many gold-splashed evergreen shrubs bleach or scorch under coastal conditions. Its broadly oval leaves carry an irregular gold-yellow center bordered by dark green, giving strong color even in the shorter days of winter. Small, powerfully sweet-fragrant creamy-white flowers open in autumn, followed by edible, tart orange-red berries that ripen the following spring and are readily taken by birds. Grow it in lean to average, well-drained soil, where it will tolerate drought, wind, and salt spray better than most broadleaf evergreens, and prune out any all-green reverted shoots promptly, since they grow more vigorously than variegated growth and will overtake the plant if ignored.
